newsitem.title: FRANCE: Clashes as far-right captures fourth French town.
newsitem.headline: Clashes as far-right captures fourth French town.

text.p: France's anti-immigration National Front won a hard-fought municipal election on Sunday, taking to four the number of southern towns it controls and touching off clashes clashes between youngsters and police.

Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen had claimed victory within minutes of polls closing in Vitrolles after a contest watched by the whole of France. He said that it showed his following was capable of becoming the country's biggest party.
Final results showed Front candidate Catherine Megret, wife of the party's number two Bruno Megret, won 52.48 percent of the vote, against Socialist Jean-Jacques Anglade's 47.52 percent.

Within minutes of the announcement, gangs of young people apparently supporting Anglade broke shop-windows outside the town hall and clashed with riot police who dispersed them with tear gas. Anglade appealed for calm.

Megret won 46.7 percent of the vote in last Sunday's first round, boosting the anti-immigration movement's score by four points since 1995. Her husband had been barred from running this time after a court found him guilty of campaign spending irregularities two years ago.
Anglade, who won re-election in 1995 by a mere 353 votes, took 37 percent last Sunday at the head of a united list of Socialists, Communists and ecologists on a 76 percent turnout.

Conservative candidate Roger Guichard scored 16.3 percent and pulled out of the second ballot at the insistence of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right national coalition, which urged a "republican vote to bar the road to the extreme-right".
Turnout was just below 81 percent, a five-point jump on the first round but too little to allow Anglade to catch up.

Only a massive switch of centre-right votes to Anglade, and a strong turnout by those who stayed away from the polls in the first round, could have stopped the Front winning depressed Vitrolles, which has a population of 40,000.
"Who can say that the National Front is not capable of becoming France's first party? If you judge from the Vitrolles microcosm, you realise that it's possible," Le Pen told Europe-1 radio.
Le Pen said that the French would come to realise "the shortcomings of those who lead them and...the failure to resolve major problems like unemployment, immigration, and taxes."
The Front said the victory -- like those in Toulon, Orange and Marignane in 1995 "open the way to a French Renaissance."

Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy, in a radio interview, urged centre-right voters to fight the Front "through militancy in the universities, unions, in daily life. If we're not capable of doing that, we'll be shattered."
Socialist chief Lionel Jospin and Communist leader Robert Hue, flanked by film stars and Jewish leaders, have appealed to Vitrolles citizens to vote against "racism and hatred".
But Socialist officials privately acknowledged that Anglade, under judicial investigation for alleged sleaze, was a poor advertisement for a party keen to shake off past graft scandals.

Bruno Megret, who plans to be his wife's chief aide, hammered home charges that France's political class is corrupt and told some 1,500 supporters at a final rally on Thursday their vote "impressed the whole of Europe".

The Front, which has played up the law-and-order issue in Vitrolles, advocates expelling some three million immigrants from France and giving preference in housing, jobs and welfare benefits to French nationals.
